items.title: Mimo V2.6 Pro & Flash (Fully Tested): This is OPEN WEIGHTS!?
items.summary:
In this video, I compare Xiaomi’s new MiMo V2.6 Pro and MiMo V2.6 Flash models across all eight KingBench 3 tasks using OpenCode and OpenRouter. I test their coding, 3D generation, game development, SVG design, math reasoning, local fine-tuning, and overall reliability to find out which model offers the best performance and value.

--
Key Takeaways:

🚀 MiMo V2.6 Pro and Flash are open-weight mixture-of-experts models with context windows of over one million tokens.
💸 MiMo V2.6 Flash is about 68 percent cheaper than Pro for standard input and output tokens.
🏢 Flash produced a more reliable elevator simulation, while Pro suffered from passenger-counting and reset bugs.
🎨 Flash created the better panda SVG, although neither model fully captured the panda taking a bite.
🎮 Both models built functional bow-and-arrow games, but they shared an input-handling bug involving the R key.
🧮 Neither model completed the original math task, though Flash made substantial progress during a larger-budget
items.author: AICodeKing
items.transcript: [music] >> Hi. Welcome to another video. So, Xiaomi has released Mimo V2.6 Pro and Mimo V2.6 Flash, and the pricing immediately caught my attention. Both are available through OpenRouter. Both have open weights, and Flash costs about a third of Pro for regular input and output tokens. But, I wanted to see what that difference actually gets you when you ask them to build things. For this video, I ran both models through OpenCode on all eight tasks in KingBench 3. We have an elevator simulation, interactive 3D object, an SVG illustration, a game, a math problem, an actual local fine-tuning task, and a working 3D wristwatch. I reviewed the generated files, opened the visual projects, and checked the behavior before giving each result a score out of 10. And there are some pretty interesting differences here. Flash handled several of the practical tasks better in this run. Pro sometimes spent much longer and still left basic problems in the result. So, let's get right into it. First, a little context. OpenRouter lists both models with a September 21 release date. And Xiaomi's announcement was updated on September 22. I'm testing them on September 24th. Pro has about 1.02 trillion total parameters with 42 billion active per token. Flash has 309 billion total with 15 billion active. These are mixture of experts models, so the active count is the portion doing the work for each token. Both have a context window of just over a million tokens. Their listing support text, image, audio, and video input with text output, and the weights are released under the MIT license. That's good to see. Today's benchmark focuses on their coding and problem-solving behavior through OpenCode and OpenRouter. Now, the pricing is pretty aggressive. At the time of this test, OpenRouter lists Pro at 43.5 cents per million input tokens and 87 cents per million output tokens. Flash is 14 cents for input and 28 cents for output. Cached input has a separate lower rate. So, for ordinary input and output, Flash is about 68% cheaper. Your final bill still depends on how much the agent thinks, how many tool calls it makes, and how much context gets reused. For the testing setup, I used Open Code version 1.18.32 with Open Router as the provider. Each task had its own fresh session and folder. Both models received the same prompt with reasoning enabled. Each task gets a score out of 10. I'll also show a separate math retest with a larger output budget because that made a difference to Flash's result. The first task is the elevator simulation. We need three elevators, each taking only one person. You should be able to spawn people on different floors, have them wait for the next available elevator, and see their destination in a tooltip. Pro gives us a recognizable simulation with the right basic controls and animated elevators. But, once I started testing the passenger counts, it broke down. In one run, 16 people had been created, yet the completed counter eventually reached 21. The dispatch code treats a reservation for elevator zero as if there is no reservation, which allows duplicate handling of the same passenger. Reset also has a problem. A trip that was already running could finish after the reset and add a passenger to the cleared counter. So, the interface looks like it is working, but the underlying state isn't reliable. I'm giving Pro seven out of 10 here. Flash does much better. I cleared the initial passengers, spawned 12, and all 12 were delivered. I also queued five people on the same floor, and they waited and got picked up properly. The destination tooltip works, too. There are still delayed callbacks that aren't fully canceled when clearing the simulation, so I wouldn't call it completely robust, but the main behavior I tested works, and Flash gets nine out of 10. Now, the second task is a 3.js contact lens case with clear left and right labels and caps that open when you click them. Both models create interactive 3D scenes, and both let you open the caps independently. But, this is where looking at an object from different angles makes a difference. Pro's closed caps are positioned partly inside the body, so the closed state doesn't really look sealed. The labels and the shape are also less convincing than they should be. It gets seven out of 10. Flash has a slightly better interaction, but the geometry underneath is still wrong. There's solid material where the lens wells should be, and the letters are partly buried in the caps. Opening a cap should reveal a usable little container, and that illusion doesn't hold up here. Flash gets seven and a half out of 10. The third task is a folding table in 3 JS. Move the slider right and it should unfold. Move it left and it should fold with smooth movement through the whole range. Both models get the main interaction working. I check the end points and several positions in between, then move the slider back again. The table changes smoothly, and you can rotate the view to inspect it, but both have mechanical problems in the middle of the animation. Pro's legs pass through the floor as the table folds. Flash's inner legs intersect, and the table doesn't stay convincingly supported. So, you can demonstrate the idea, but the motion needs work before it looks physically believable. I'm giving both eight out of 10. Next is the SVG of a panda eating a burger. This sounds simple, but it checks whether the model understands the relationship between the objects, rather than just putting a panda and a burger in the same picture. Flash makes a clean recognizable illustration. The panda and burger both look good, but the burger sits beside the mouth with a visible gap. It looks more like holding food than taking a bite. That's eight out of 10. Pro adds more shading and detail, but the burger becomes an oversized stack with floating gaps between the ingredients. It also hides the mouth, which weakens the eating pose. I prefer Flash's result here. Pro gets seven out of 10. A static SVG could have earned full marks. Animation wasn't required. There's also a big timing difference on this particular task. Flash finished in about 34 seconds, while Pro took about 10 minutes. That's the total time for those agent runs, including their work and tool use. It isn't a measurement of raw token speed, and I wouldn't assume the same gap will happen on every prompt. The fifth task is the bow and arrow game. There should be four targets, and completing the challenge faster should move you higher on the leaderboard. Both models produce playable-looking games with aiming, arrows, targets, and a timer. Flash responds to a browser drag, fires an arrow, and registers a target hit. Pro has a more elaborate presentation, although its header timer can freeze while the timer drawn inside the game keeps moving. I also checked the original game logic with control simulations. Those checks completed all four targets, tested misses and repeated hits, and verified that lower completion times rank above higher ones. The more serious problem is one both models share. The R key restarts the game even when you're typing a player name, so entering a name with that letter can throw away a finished run before you save it. It's a small piece of code with a pretty annoying effect for the person playing. I'm giving Pro eight and a half out of 10, and Flash nine out of 10. Both have a solid core here with a fixable input handling bug. Flash also keeps the visible timer behaving more consistently in the version I tested. Now, the sixth task is the permutation counting problem. The correct answer is 20,460, and I independently checked that with an exhaustive program. Neither model received the answer or the checking code. The first runs didn't deliver an answer. Flash used almost 32,000 reasoning tokens and stopped because it hit the output limit. Pro reached the 20-minute time limit without returning a usable response. So, both original attempts get zero for this task. That means no delivered answer under these conditions, rather than a specific wrong number. There is an important setup detail here. Open code had a default output cap of 32,000 tokens, even though these models advertise support for up to 131,072 output tokens. I therefore gave both models one fresh retest with that larger cap, the same prompt, and the same 20-minute time limit. I kept those results separate, so we're not quietly replacing a failed attempt with a better-looking one. In that retest, Pro still delivered nothing before timeout. Flash wrote a valid counting program and checks on smaller versions support its method, but it never ran the program or gave the final number. That earns six out of 10 in partial credit on the retest. Its original attempt remains zero, and I'll show the effect of replacing that score separately. The seventh task is the local fine-tuning task. Generate a panda fact dataset, fine-tune Gemma 2B, and build a local webpage that generates a panda fact whenever you refresh it. I've tried both implementations, and they work flawlessly. Both handle the fine-tuning workflow and deliver the local fact generation app the prompt asks for. Refresh the page and you get a panda fact from the model. So, this is a full pass for both. Pro gets 10 out of 10, and Flash gets 10 out of 10. This is a good result because the task goes beyond making an interface. It includes preparing the data, training the model, and connecting it to a working local app. Both models get the job done here. Finally, we have the working 3D wrist watch with smooth hands and two time zones. Pro's watch opens and runs. The time zone values are correct, the hands show the right time, and you can swap the zones. It also models the case, strap, and a wrist. Unfortunately, the dial markings are hidden under solid case geometry. You can see the hands moving over what looks like a blank metal face. The second hand sweeps smoothly, but the minute and hour hands advance in small steps. Pro gets eight out of 10. Flash initially looks more complete with a detailed face and a second zone subdial. But, the digital readouts and analog hands don't agree. Its code already includes fractional minutes and hours, then adds those fractions again when positioning the hands. The hour hand runs visibly ahead, and the formulas also produce backward jumps at time boundaries. The digital zones themselves are correct, and the second hand moves smoothly, but accurate hands are central to a working watch, and part of the lower strap also disappears through the floor. Flash gets six and a half out of 10. This is a good example of why I check the behavior after the first screenshot. So, this is the updated final chart. Pro gets 55 and 1/2 out of 80, which is about 6.94 out of 10 overall. Flash gets 58 out of 80, which is 7.25 out of 10. If we use this separately labeled larger budget math retest, Pro stays at about 6.94, while Flash rises to 64 out of 80 or 8 out of 10. Both totals include full marks for the fine-tuning task. Now, in percentage terms, Mimo V2.6 Pro scores 69.38% and Flash scores 72.5% ahead of GPT-5.6, Soul and Muse Spark 1.3 at 71.25% but below GLM-5.2 at 75% With the larger budget math retest, Flash reaches 80%. That matches the previous Opus-4.8 score, puts it above GLM-5.3, Flash at 78.75% and leaves it just below DeepSeek V4.1, Flash at 81.25%. So, Flash's retest result moves it into a much stronger part of the table, while Pro remains at 69.38%. Combined with Flash's lower pricing, that makes it the more interesting result for me here. Both models earn full marks on local fine-tuning. Flash takes the overall lead through its stronger elevator simulation, illustration, and game, while Pro does better on the watch. If you ask me, Flash is the more interesting value option from these results. It has much lower token prices and I preferred its elevator simulation, panda illustration, and game. Pro did better on the watch's timekeeping, so there are real differences rather than one model winning every task. Personally, I'd try Flash first for inexpensive prototypes and inspect the result carefully. This run doesn't give me a strong reason to pay extra for Pro by default. Both can produce useful starting points, but the geometry bugs, state bugs, and math results still need attention. Overall, it's pretty cool. Anyway, let me know your thoughts in the comments. If you like [music] this video, consider donating through the Super Thanks option or becoming a member by clicking the join button. Also, [music] give this video a thumbs up and subscribe to my channel. I'll see you in the next one. Until then, bye. >> [music]

In this video, I’ll show you how to use Claude Code Templates to discover, inspect, and install agents, skills, commands, MCPs, hooks, and settings. We’ll build a practical code-review and testing workflow, explore the analytics dashboard and conversation monitor, and discuss what to check before adding community templates to your projects.

--
Key Takeaways:

🔍 Claude Code Templates provides a searchable catalog of agents, skills, commands, MCPs, hooks, settings, mods, and plugins.
🛠️ The Stack Builder lets you select multiple components and generate one combined installation command.

items.author: AICodeKing
items.transcript: Hi. Welcome to another video. So, your coding agent can read your project, edit files, and run tests. But, when it needs to know how a library actually behaves, where is that information coming from? Maybe it remembers the right answer. Maybe it finds an old tutorial. And sometimes you get a very confident explanation followed by another broken patch. Today, we're looking at Octon as a search tool for coding agents. Specifically, how to connect it skills to Codex or Claude code, when to use search versus extraction, and what changes when you bring documentation into the actual editing and testing process. I installed the core skills in a separate project, checked whether Codex could discover Octon search, and ran two small coding exercises. We'll look at the code before and after, the test results, and a mistake from Octon's public demo that shows why reading the source still matters. The headline is pretty interesting. In Artificial Analysis' September 22nd snapshot, Octon with highlights shares the third highest quality score at 77. It also has the fastest reported query latency, around 0.21 seconds, and the fastest task time figure on that board. Its search spend was $9.07 per thousand benchmark tasks, compared with $65.57 for ExaAuto. That's roughly 1/7. Include model costs, though, and the saving is about 54%. This is a search agent benchmark, so it gives us a reason to investigate Octon. It doesn't tell us how many more coding tasks your agent will solve. And on that board, Octon is the only listed search vendor that sits in the top three for quality, speed, and search cost at the same time. What I'd call practical soda, not just winning one metric. For me, the useful question is what the agent does with those search results. A link is only the beginning. I want it to find the right version of the documentation, identify the behavior that matters, and turn that into a change we can verify. So, let's get right into it. The Octon skills repository gives your existing agent instructions for using Octon's APIs. You keep working in your normal coding tool. The skills explain how to search, how to read a known page, and which operation fits the task. There are six skills in the repository. For this workflow, start with three. Octant web search, which handles routing, Octant search, which performs searches, and Octant extract, which reads pages from URLs. The other three cover image search, video search, and design references and currently require invite-only beta access. That routing part matters more than it sounds. If you're checking one API behavior, use a focused search. If you already have the documentation URL, extract that page. If you're researching a larger decision with several distinct questions, broad search can expand the investigation. For example, checking where Python raises a timeout exception is one focused lookup. Evaluating several database options across hosting, licensing, migration effort, and runtime compatibility is a broader research task. You don't need the same amount of searching for both. The benefit for a coding agent is having this process available inside the task. It can inspect the dependency version, get the matching documentation, and continue editing with that evidence. The potential benefit for you is less manual switching between your editor, search results, and documentation tabs. Now, let's configure it. First, open a terminal in the project where you want to use Octant. You'll need Node and NPM for the repository's recommended install command. For Codex, run NPX skills add followed by Octant-team/octant-skills and then -a codex. For Claude code, use the same repository and change the agent argument to -a Claude-code. The exact commands are in the companion notes, including a version that selects only the three core skills. Without -g, you're installing for the project. Add -g if you want a user-wide installation. I prefer starting in one project so I can check the behavior before making it part of every coding session. For my installation test, I copied the three official skill folders into the demo projects.agents/skills directory using the skill installer. I then launched a fresh Codex session and explicitly asked it to use Octant search. Codex found the skill in its available metadata and read its instructions. That confirms skill discovery. Authentication is the next step. Create an API key in your Octant account and make it available as the environment variable named Octant_API_Key. In Claude code, you can put it in the env section of the projects.claude/settings.local.json file. If you create that file yourself, make sure it's ignored by Git. For Codex, the repository documents the user-level config.toml file inside.codex. Add the key through the shell environment policy section using its set mapping. Merge that into your existing configuration, then start a fresh session. The companion notes have the exact toml example. Check that the agent sees the variable without printing the key, then ask for one narrow documentation search and inspect which tool or API it actually called. A successful installation message by itself doesn't prove the agent used Octant for the task, and you don't have to configure an MCP server for this route. These skills include direct HTTP instructions. Octant also offers a hosted MCP endpoint if you prefer that integration, but it's optional and configured separately. I had already used Octant's public search demo, so I took the official documentation it surfaced, checked the relevant passages, and handed those notes to Codex for the coding exercises. The handoff was manual. These are real code edits and real test runs, but they are not an authenticated end-to-end Octant skill benchmark. I want that distinction clear before we look at the results. For the first exercise, we have a small asynchronous Python helper. It runs an operation with a deadline and should return a cached value if that deadline expires. The starting code catches timeout error inside the timeout context. It looks reasonable at a glance. There's a timeout, a try block, and a fallback. But, the slow operation test errors instead of returning the cached value. The documentation explains the missing detail. The timeout context handles cancellation and converts it into timeout error as the context exits. That resulting exception needs to be caught outside the context. Octon's public demo got this rule right and surfaced the official Python documentation. For the coding run, I supplied that source note and asked Codex for a minimal repair. The change moves the try block around the entire timeout context with the exception handler outside it. We keep the same function and the same intended behavior. Now, run the tests. The slow operation returns the fallback. The fast operation preserves its original result, and an unrelated value error still propagates. All three checks pass. That last check matters. A patch that catches every exception might make the timeout test green while hiding another bug. We want the specific failure handled without swallowing unrelated errors. The rule was checked against Python 3.1 documentation, and the actual tests ran on Python 3.1.14. So, keep the documentation version and the test runtime visible when you're recording something like this. The second exercise is SQLite, and this one shows why the order of operations can be more important than adding more code. We have an in-memory database with a parent table and a child table. The child declares a foreign key. Our setup opens a connection, begins a transaction, and then tries to enable foreign key enforcement. The baseline tests show the problem. The setting is still off, and inserting a child with missing parent succeeds. A valid parent and child insert also works. So, testing only the happy path would miss this. The official SQLite documentation explains that changing this setting during an active transaction has no effect. Codex moves the enable statement before the transaction begins. That's the essential change. Run the same tests again. Enforcement now reports enabled. A valid relationship is accepted and an orphan insert raises an integrity error. All three checks pass using SQLite 3.53.1 in this environment. So, across the two exercises, the starting fixtures passed three of six checks. After the changes, all six passed. The tests stayed the same and the original files are preserved, so you can inspect the exact diff. These bugs were deliberately seeded. They were not mistakes produced by a competing model and we didn't run an otherwise identical agent without the evidence. The result demonstrates two verified repairs. It doesn't establish a percentage improvement from adding Octon. What I like about this workflow is that the explanation connects to something observable. We have the source rule, the line that changed, and a test that exercises the behavior. That's much more useful during a code review than a long answer with several links attached. >> Now, the SQLite search also exposed a problem. Octon's public answer identified the transaction issue, but it added advice about deferring foreign key checks that could be mistaken for another way to enable enforcement. Those are different operations. I checked that extra suggestion against the source before preparing the coding handoff. And in a separate Cloudflare question, the demo produced an incorrect timeout explanation, even though the official documentation appeared in its search results. So, having the right page in the result list does not guarantee that the generated answer uses it correctly. For your coding agent, I would make the prompt specific, ask it to inspect the project's versions, use Octon to find the relevant official documentation, read the passage that determines the behavior, then make the smallest change and run the existing tests. Ask it to show the source and the resulting diff. For a dependency upgrade, give it both the version you're on and the version you're moving to. Have it identify the changes that affect your code, check those against the migration guide, and and each edit. A current webpage can still describe a version your project doesn't use. For an unfamiliar integration, use search to locate the official API reference and extraction to read the selected pages. Keep the returned content focused on the methods and constraints you need. Pulling a huge pile of vaguely related documentation into the context can make the task harder to follow. And if the source doesn't support the proposed fix, the agent should say what's missing. It can run a targeted experiment or refine the lookup. Repeating broader searches isn't automatically progress. Now, there are also some useful changes in the skills repository itself. The revision I checked was from September 1. During August, the project removed the bundled MCP configuration from the Codex package, leaving a skills-only setup. Later documentation added the hosted MCP option. That explains why you may see different setup instructions in older examples. The routing instructions also make focused search the default for a narrow question and reserve broad search for work that needs several research angles. That's useful for coding because a small documentation question shouldn't turn into a large research job every time. There were API documentation corrections, too, including removal of unsupported image search time filters. That's a practical reason to update installed skills. An agent can follow an outdated parameter example perfectly and still get behavior you didn't intend. If you install through the skills CLI, NPX skills update is the update command. Review the changes and repeat a small search check afterward. If you copied the folders manually, refresh those copies from the repository instead. For front-end work, the design skill is an interesting extension. It can retrieve visual references and, where available, structured style information and HTML or CSS snippets. The intended workflow is to inspect those references and adapt them to your project's components and design choices. I didn't test the live design endpoint, which also requires beta access. I did run the repository's existing 27 design helper tests against its local mock server, and all 27 passed. Those tests cover things like partial API failures, malformed responses, retries, and thumbnail fallbacks. Recent fixes preserve successful references when another request fails and report the error separately. That's helpful because an agent needs to distinguish an empty result from a failed request before deciding what to do next. Now, let's talk about the cost. Because a coding agent can make a lot of tool calls over a long task, Octane's pricing page currently advertises a promotional $1 per 1,000 web search queries. Exa lists $7 per 1,000 for its base search tier with up to 10 results. Under those assumptions, 10,000 searches would be $10 versus $70 before additional charges or model usage. Tavily's basic pay-as-you-go search works out to $8 per 1,000 at its listed credit price. Parallel's fast and turbo modes start at $1 per 1,000, while basic and advanced are $5. So, Octane has an attractive price, but Parallel already competes at that entry point. Broad search also bills generated subqueries. One request that expands into five searches isn't the same cost as one focused search. That's another reason I like the routing approach for coding tasks. If you already have Exa, Tavily, or Parallel in your stack, compare a few real tasks before switching. A version-specific bug, a dependency migration, and an unfamiliar API integration. Track whether the agent found the relevant source, whether the patch passed, how many searches it made, and the total task cost. Personally, I think Octane is most interesting when your coding agent regularly needs external documentation, and you want an inexpensive search option with explicit instructions for using it. The public benchmark is encouraging, and the source-to-patch workflow is useful. The live skill integration still needs an authenticated test before I can judge that whole experience. For this test, the concrete results are that Codex discovered the core search skill, the two seated repairs passed all six checks, and the design helper passed its 27 local regression tests. The files and commands are included, so you can inspect what happened and reproduce the coding examples. Start with the three core skills, check one real documentation lookup, and then try it on a task where the external information actually matters. That's where I would look for the benefit. Overall, it's pretty cool. >> Anyway, let me know your thoughts in the comments. If you like this video, consider donating through the Super Thanks option or becoming a member by clicking the join button. Also, give this video a thumbs up and subscribe to my channel. I'll see you in the next one. Until then, bye.

In this video, I’ll show you the new Command Code desktop app and test whether its affordable Go and GOAT plans can serve as practical alternatives to expensive AI coding subscriptions. We’ll use DeepSeek V4 Flash to build a dashboard feature, review its plan, run tests, inspect the changes, and explore tools like Browser, Design mode, and Taste.

--
Key Takeaways:

💻 Command Code now offers a desktop app for macOS, Windows, and Linux with the agent runtime included.
💸 Its Go plan starts at $1 per month, while the GOAT plan starts at $10 per month, plus processing fees.
🤖 You can choose from affordable coding models such as DeepSeek, GLM, Kimi, and Qwen.
🧪 DeepSeek V4 Flash successfully built a search and filtering feature with eleven passing tests.
📝 Plan mode lets you review, refine, and approve an implementation plan before the agent edits your code.
🎨 Browser
items.author: AICodeKing
items.transcript: [music] >> Hi, welcome to another video. So, if you've been looking at the $200 plans from OpenAI and Claude and thinking, "I just want a good coding agent without another massive monthly bill." Command Code now has a desktop app, and this is a pretty interesting option. I've covered Command Code on the channel before, including their $1 Go Plan and the 10 Go Plan. But, having that agent inside a proper visual workspace makes the whole thing much easier to show and much easier to get started with. You can work on your project, inspect the code, and see what you're building. And you can choose from models like DeepSeek, GLM, Kimmy, and Quinn while keeping the monthly starting cost extremely low. So, I opened the app and gave DeepSeek V4 Flash a small dashboard feature to build. It finished with 11 passing tests, and I checked the search and filtering myself inside its browser. There were a few rough edges along the way, which I'll show you, too. Let's walk through that workflow and talk about where this could make sense as an alternative to those expensive subscriptions. So, let's get right into it. First, a quick clarification on the comparison. The $200 options I'm talking about are ChatGPT Pro's higher tier, which includes Codex, and Claude Max 20X. Both companies also have cheaper plans, including $20 options. So, you don't need to spend $200 just to use their coding tools. But, if you're considering that upgrade mainly to get more coding done, I think it's worth looking at how much of your work a cheaper setup could handle first. Now, to install Command Code, go to their desktop page. They have downloads for macOS, Windows, and Linux. On a Mac, download the DMG, open it, and move the app into applications. On Windows, follow the setup installer. And on supported Linux systems, use the package for your distribution. The agent runtime is included, so you don't need to separately install their CLI before using the desktop app. That's a nice improvement for anyone who wasn't interested in setting up another terminal tool. I'm using the installed app here, already signed in. To add the demo, I opened the add project menu, selected open folder, and chose a small disposable project. That's the flow in the build I'm using. The layout is pretty straightforward. Your projects and chats live on the left, the conversation is in the middle, and the workbench sits on the right. Open a view gives you files, changes, browser, and plan. Terminal opens as a drawer underneath the chat, so you can keep your server running while reviewing the page. For this walk-through, let's use a small dashboard project and add search and filtering to a list of tasks. Something practical that gives us a bit of interface work and a bit of application logic. First, open the model picker in the composer. The models are grouped by provider, and there are search and favorite controls. For this test, I used DeepSeek v4 flash with max effort. Its picker also showed default and high, so you can adjust that from the interface. Now, switch into plan mode and give it the request. I'll say, "Inspect this project and plan how to add search and status filters to the task list. Reuse the existing components and styling. Search should ignore capitalization, and it should work together with the status filter. Include an empty state when nothing matches, and explain how you'll test it." This is the kind of prompt I like, because it gives the agent a clear finish line. A search box that looks good but doesn't work with the filter would still be an incomplete feature. The agent read the project and opened its proposal in the plan panel. There are buttons for accept and build, keep refining, and build without asking. And this is where I actually used keep refining. The first plan had the substring comparison written in the wrong direction, and one paragraph was unclear about clearing filters. I wanted clearing the search to preserve the selected status, and only the clear filters button to reset everything. So, I sent that feedback through the review panel. It revised the plan, opened version two, and highlighted what changed. That's pretty cool. You get a proper place to review the approach before it becomes code. Then I chose accept and build. That returned the chat to ask for approval, and I approved the changes to the demo files as it worked. The activity feed showed the edits and commands, so I could follow what was happening. Now, while that's running, let's talk about why the agent around the model matters. A coding model has to do more than write a convincing answer. It needs to request the right files, make usable edits, understand command output, and keep working when something goes wrong. Command code has published details about its tool call repair system. Their approach is to validate the arguments a model sends to a tool and repair certain malformed calls when validation fails. Valid calls are left alone.
